title: Final review week
intro: Use this plan in the last 7 days before CIA Part 2, after you have worked through the notes and taken your mocks. Nothing in it is new: the week sharpens what you already know. Most days take about an hour; the two mock days take longer.
how_it_works: No new topics this week. Late new material crowds out what you have already learned.
One full timed mock at the start of the week, then no more full mocks. The last days are for recall and rest.
Answer from memory first, then check. Recalling builds memory; rereading mostly makes pages feel familiar.
Time follows the exam weights, so Section A, half the exam, gets the most, then Section B. Section C gets a short, steady share.
Part 2 turns on close pairs: approve or tell, design or operation, symptom or cause. A few minutes a day on these pairs keeps them apart.
Memory settles while you sleep, so a full night's rest is part of the plan. Missed a day? Skip it and carry on; never double up.

days.title: Full rehearsal
days.goal: Sit one full timed mock at the real length, ideally at your exam's start time, to rehearse pace and stamina.

tasks.text: Take a full timed mock in one sitting: 100 questions in 120 minutes, phone away, no notes.
Pace by two checkpoints, not by timing each question: question 50 by minute 60; question 75 by minute 90.
Stuck on one? Choose your best answer, flag it and move on. Wrong answers are not penalized on the real exam.
Your misses go to your mistake journal on their own. Rest tonight and review them tomorrow.

days.remember: A mock is a rehearsal, not a verdict. KaiSip shows percent by section; that is not The IIA's scaled score and cannot predict your result.

days.title: Learn from your misses
days.goal: Trace each mock miss to its thinking slip, then recall Section A, half the exam. Stop at about 90 minutes.

tasks.text: In your mistake journal, review each miss from the mock, newest first.
Tag why you missed each one: “Acted as the wrong person”, “Missed FIRST or BEST”, “Tool before policy”, “Fixed the symptom, not the cause”, “Misread” or “Didn’t know it”.
Read the principles behind the slip you tagged most often.
From memory, list five Section A points in engagement order, from objectives to resources. Then open the list and check.
Read the principles on your seat: who sets the scope, who approves, and who owns the fix.

days.remember: A miss you understand is worth more than a right answer you guessed.

days.title: The three close pairs
days.goal: Drill the pairs Part 2 turns on, recall Section B, and work on the section furthest behind its weight.

tasks.text: Approve or tell: say who approves a change of scope or of the work program, and who must be told in time. Then check the note.
Design or operation: say which question comes first for a control, and what an interview alone can prove. Then check the principle.
Symptom or cause: take one miss from your journal and ask why until you reach a cause. Then check the note.
From memory, list three Section B points on evidence and findings. Then open the list and check.
Answer a short untimed set in your focus section. Before each answer, name the engagement stage and the actor.

days.remember: The chief audit executive or a delegated supervisor approves; management is told in time. Design before operation; cause before symptom.

days.title: Pace check
days.goal: Keep your pace sharp with one short timed mock, then recall the order of planning, what makes evidence enough and who may staff the work.

tasks.text: Take the short timed mock in one sitting. Watch your pace more than the score.
Without looking, say the planning steps that come before any testing, in order. Then check the principles on what drives the work.
From memory, say what makes the work program adequate and when it must be approved. Then check the note.
Read the principles on proving it: relevant, reliable and sufficient evidence, root cause and design against operation.
Say why staff from the area under review may not test it, and who hears about an impairment. Then check the principles on staying unbiased.

days.remember: This is your last timed test before the exam. From here, short recall keeps you sharp.

days.title: Supervision and speaking up
days.goal: Recall Section C from the engagement auditor's seat, sharpen how you read questions, and work on your second gap.

tasks.text: From memory, list three Section C points and say who acts in each. Then open the list and check.
Read the principles on speaking up: the right channel, the right order and the plain truth.
Read the principles on reading the question.
Practice a short untimed set in your second-weakest section. Find the priority word before you read the options.
Redo your mistake journal questions. Before you choose, say why your old answer loses.

days.remember: An urgent issue is raised during the engagement. Reaching the board is the chief audit executive's step, never the engagement auditor's.

days.title: Light review and logistics
days.goal: Touch everything once, lightly, and settle the practical details so nothing on the day is a surprise.

tasks.text: For each section, recall two points before you open its list, starting with Section A. Spend a few minutes, not an hour.
Say the seven priority words and the answering steps from memory, then check them.
Say the three pairs once more: approve or tell, design or operation, symptom or cause. Then glance at the one-line rules.
Look up any term on the lists that still feels fuzzy.
Confirm your appointment, the test center's address and your route. Read the ID and check-in rules in The IIA's candidate handbook.

days.remember: Recall beats rereading. Leave new material alone now.

days.title: The eve
days.goal: Stay fresh, not tired: a light touch in the morning, then rest.

tasks.text: Optional: say the answering steps and your two checkpoints from memory, then check them. Stop after 15 minutes.
Read the one-line rule for your most common slip on the principles list.
Work through the eve checklist.
Close the books by early evening and keep your usual bedtime.

days.remember: Rest is part of the plan. If sleep comes slowly tonight, that is common, and your preparation is already done.

eve: Your appointment is confirmed, and you have read the ID and check-in rules in The IIA's current candidate handbook.
Your route to the test center and your travel time are planned, with a backup.
Your ID is laid out where you will see it in the morning.
You have read the reminder for your most common slip.
Skip alcohol tonight; it makes sleep lighter.
If worries keep circling, write them down for a few minutes, then put the page away.
Books are closed by early evening, and you keep your usual bedtime.
morning: Eat a familiar breakfast and keep your usual caffeine.
Reread your two checkpoints: question 50 by minute 60; question 75 by minute 90.
Leave early enough that a delay on the way would not matter.
Remind yourself of your seat: the internal auditor running one engagement. You plan, test and conclude; approvals go to the chief audit executive, and the fix stays with management.
A racing heart is your body getting ready. Treat it as energy for focus, not a sign of danger.
If your mind goes blank, breathe out slowly, pick your best answer for now and move on.

points.text: Objectives: the internal auditor builds them from the activity's strategy, risks and processes, with management's input, and fits them to assurance or advisory work. The chief audit executive or a delegated supervisor approves them.

Scope covers every objective. When an assurance scope covers a Topical Requirement's topic, each requirement is assessed and any exclusion is recorded with a reason. Management's preference is never that reason.
A change to objectives or scope during the work needs approval first and timely word to management. Never widen or trim the work quietly.
Adequate criteria set by the board and senior management must be used. If they are inadequate, better ones are worked out with senior management, the board or both. Criteria are fixed before testing.

The engagement's own risk assessment comes before the work program: fraud included, last cycle's list reviewed and updated, and risks ranked by impact and likelihood, never by how easy they are to test.

The work program is approved before fieldwork, and every change promptly; agile and remote approaches keep that rule. Within it, judge whether a control's design could work before testing how it operates.
Short of people, skills, money or time: raise it with the chief audit executive. A smaller scope is an approved change. Never borrow staff from the area under review to test it.

Statements describe; inspection, observation, reperformance and data show. Evidence is more reliable when the internal auditor obtains evidence directly or independently, when it is corroborated, and when its source system is well controlled.

Evidence must be relevant, reliable and sufficient. More of it never repairs evidence that is off the point or untrustworthy. If relevant evidence cannot be obtained, decide whether that gap is itself a finding.
Analytics start from the question, then relevant, normalized data. A ratio, trend, variance or flag is a lead; only follow-up against the criteria turns it into a potential finding.

A finding is the condition measured against the criteria. Ask why until you reach the cause, identify it with management where possible, and state the effect. Staff not following a procedure is usually the symptom.
Significance is likelihood and impact in context, not the size of the number. Nature, recurrence and legal or safety effects can make a small amount significant.
A complete workpaper lets a competent stranger repeat the work and reach the same result: the population, the items that passed, the method, and a trail from each finding to its evidence.

A conclusion weighs the findings together, not by count, against the engagement's objectives. For assurance it says how effective the processes are, including when they work. A list of findings is not a conclusion.

Supervision starts at planning and runs to sign-off, as closely as the auditor's experience and the engagement's complexity need. The chief audit executive may delegate the work, never the accountability.
Before results go out, the supervisor confirms the workpapers support every finding, conclusion and recommendation. A doubtful conclusion gets a request for evidence, not a quiet rewrite.
Every auditor gets feedback on their work. Judge the quality of evidence, reasoning and communication, not the number of findings raised, which can bias objectivity.
Match the form to the weight: oral and informal exchanges are normal, but a significant matter goes in writing, and key discussions are recorded in the workpapers.
Communicate from the engagement notice through fieldwork, and discuss results before the final communication. An issue that needs immediate attention is raised now, while management can still act.

Escalate by the matter: a scope limitation to management first, then the chief audit executive elevates it; resource gaps and impairments to the chief audit executive. Reaching the board is the chief audit executive's step.
Send each message to the people who must act or oversee, at the level that can change the process. Confidential information goes only to authorized parties.

principles.intro: The mindset principles, one line each. Read a few a day this week, starting with the family behind your most common slip.

priority_words.meaning: Order. Engagement steps run in sequence: understand the activity, assess its risks, set objectives, scope and criteria, approve the work program, then test. Discussion comes before escalation.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which step does this one depend on?

priority_words.meaning: Several options would help. Pick the one that keeps you in the engagement auditor's seat: it gathers or judges evidence, reaches the cause, and leaves approval and action with their owners.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which one keeps me in my seat?

priority_words.meaning: A ranking on one named quality, such as MOST reliable evidence or MOST relevant criteria. Judge the options on that quality only.
The main purpose or reason, not a side benefit. A work program exists to achieve the engagement objectives; a walk-through exists to confirm how the process really runs.
priority_words.cue: Ask: why does this exist at all?

priority_words.meaning: The largest amount of the named quality. For a risk or a finding, weigh likelihood and impact together against the activity's objectives, not the money involved alone.
priority_words.cue: Ask: greatest what, and for which objective?

priority_words.meaning: Probability, not severity. What the facts given most probably point to, such as the likely root cause behind a pattern of exceptions, even if another outcome would be worse.
priority_words.cue: Ask: what usually follows from these facts?

priority_words.meaning: Flip the test. Three options fit, and you want the one that helps or fits least. Slow down when you see it.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which one does not belong?

answering_routine.title: Read the last line first
answering_routine.text: Find what is asked: an action, a person, a document, a test or a reason.

answering_routine.title: Place the engagement stage
answering_routine.text: Planning, fieldwork, concluding or communicating? An option that belongs to another stage, or skips one, is often the trap.

answering_routine.title: Find the actor and the priority word
answering_routine.text: Internal auditor, engagement supervisor, chief audit executive or the management of the activity? Then spot FIRST, BEST, MOST, PRIMARY, GREATEST, MOST LIKELY or LEAST before you read the options.

answering_routine.title: Eliminate two
answering_routine.text: Strike options where the auditor fixes or decides for management, a step is skipped or left unapproved, a statement is treated as proof, or a should is called a must.

answering_routine.title: Settle the final two with a principle
answering_routine.text: Ask what comes first, who approves, whether another competent auditor would accept the evidence, and which option reaches the cause. Say the reason in one sentence, then answer.

pace: 100 questions in 120 minutes is 1.2 minutes each. Use that to set checkpoints, not to time each question.
Checkpoints: question 50 by minute 60; question 75 by minute 90. Look at the clock there and otherwise leave it alone.
Ahead at a checkpoint? Those minutes are your review time. Behind? Decide a little faster on the next few; do not rush them all.
Stuck? Choose your best answer and move on. Wrong answers are not penalized, so never leave a blank.
No breaks are scheduled, and the clock keeps running if you take one.
Change an answer when you find a clear reason, such as an actor, a stage or a priority word you missed the first time.
